summaries.example: Imagine choosing whether to join a game. You listen to your friends, think about what you want, and then decide. That is different from someone forcing you or from a powerful urge that makes choosing feel impossible. The philosophers in this entry ask what makes a choice truly your own.
summaries.summary: Personal autonomy means governing yourself. When you act, you must use your own judgment in some way, because you are the one who starts the action. But having this special authority over yourself does not guarantee that you are really in control. Desires, habits, pressure, addiction, brainwashing, tiredness, or other forces may interfere with self-government. Philosophers offer several ideas about what autonomy requires. Some say your actions should fit with your deeper wishes, values, plans, or cares. Others say you must be able to notice and respond to reasons, or think carefully about your beliefs and desires. Another view says outside causes can make autonomy impossible. The entry explains that each idea has difficulties. For example, a person can act against a plan and still make a choice, and a person can make a mistaken choice while remaining its author. The central question is how to distinguish ordinary influences on action from influences that take away genuine self-government.
key_ideas: Autonomy means more than simply doing what you want. It involves having some real power to guide your actions.
Every person who acts must use their own judgment in deciding what to do, even when other people give advice.
Philosophers disagree about what can weaken self-government, including pressure, addiction, brainwashing, or difficulty thinking clearly.
A person may act against a long-term plan and still have some autonomy. Being inconsistent does not automatically mean a choice is not one’s own.
The entry does not settle the debate. It shows why the idea of self-government is difficult to define.
summaries.why_it_matters: Thinking about autonomy helps us understand choice, responsibility, and respect. It reminds us that helping someone decide is different from taking control away. It also shows why judging people’s actions can be complicated: a person may make a bad or mistaken choice without losing all power over it, while another person may act under a force that seriously undermines self-government.

important_terms.definition: Being able to guide your own actions and make decisions as yourself.
A person or being that acts and makes things happen.
The power or right to decide what you will do.
Thinking about what you believe, want, or have reason to do.

questions_to_think_about: If someone gives you advice, how can you tell whether you are still making your own decision?
Can a choice be your own even when it is a poor choice?
What is the difference between being influenced and being controlled?
Can making a plan help you guide your future actions?
Why might it be hard to tell whether a strong urge comes from you or takes over your choice?

summaries.example: Suppose a student has decided to study for an exam but later chooses to play games instead. This may conflict with a long-term plan, yet the choice could still be autonomous: the student may recognize the conflict and deliberately abandon the plan. Compare this with a case in which a compulsive urge overwhelms the student’s ability to resist, or in which someone has manipulated the student’s thinking so thoroughly that the student cannot meaningfully question the motive. The cases raise different questions about control, reflection, and authorship.
summaries.summary: The entry examines personal autonomy as self-government: the relation in which an agent’s motives and actions are attributable to the agent’s own power to determine what to do. Agency itself supplies a kind of authority. Whenever we decide, we must treat some judgment as action-guiding, even if that judgment tells us to follow another person’s advice. Yet this authority can become merely formal: motives may move us in ways that bypass or undermine our capacity to govern ourselves. The entry surveys four overlapping families of accounts. Coherentist views locate autonomy in harmony between motivating states and higher-order desires, evaluative judgments, plans, cares, or character. Reasons-responsive views require sensitivity to relevant practical considerations. Responsiveness-to-reasoning views focus on the ability to reflect on and revise one’s motives, while relational views emphasize the social and psychological conditions of self-respect and self-trust. Incompatibilist views hold that causal determination by forces outside the agent’s control defeats autonomy; compatibilist views maintain that determined action can still be autonomous. Each account faces difficulties. Endorsement may itself be manipulated, coherence is not required for every autonomous choice, ignorance does not automatically remove authorship, and the proposed standards may confuse ideal agency with the minimum needed for accountability. A Kant-influenced alternative emphasizes the practical point of view: facts may cause a decision without dictating the significance the agent must assign to them. The entry concludes that autonomy is central to responsibility and political claims to self-rule, but its minimal conditions remain elusive.
key_ideas: Agency gives each person a special authority over their own action, but that authority does not guarantee effective control over their motives.
Coherentist theories connect autonomy with endorsement or harmony among levels of desire, evaluation, plans, cares, or character.
Reasons-responsive theories require sensitivity to relevant considerations; reasoning-responsive theories instead emphasize the capacity to evaluate and revise one’s motives.
Relational approaches stress that self-respect and self-trust, often shaped by social relationships, can be necessary for a genuinely owned point of view.
Incompatibilist theories argue that causal determination by forces beyond the agent’s control undermines autonomy, while compatibilist theories deny that determination alone has this result.
The entry stresses a threshold problem: theories of ideal self-government may not identify the minimal conditions needed for an agent to be responsible for an intentional action.
summaries.why_it_matters: Autonomy matters because it connects personal choice with accountability, respect, and political self-rule. The concept helps distinguish ordinary causal influence from coercion, manipulation, addiction, or other conditions that may undermine self-government. It also cautions against simple judgments: poor reasoning, weakness of will, or acting against one’s values may reduce the quality of self-government without eliminating agency altogether. Understanding these distinctions is important whenever we ask whether a person truly authored an action and what responsibilities follow.

important_terms.definition: Self-government: an agent’s exercise of authority over the motives and actions that directly produce behavior.
A being capable of initiating action; in the entry, an agent’s own practical judgments have a distinctive authority because the agent acts.
The power to determine how one will act. The entry distinguishes possessing this status from actually controlling the forces that move one.
A view that autonomy requires harmony between a person’s motivating desire and higher-order attitudes, values, plans, cares, or character.
A view that autonomous motives or the processes producing them must respond to a sufficiently broad range of reasons for and against action.
A view emphasizing the ability to assess one’s motives through one’s beliefs and desires and revise them through practical reasoning.
The position that autonomy is incompatible with actions being fully determined by causes outside the agent’s control.
The standpoint from which a person decides what to do by considering facts and assigning them practical significance, rather than merely predicting events.

questions_to_think_about: Is endorsing a desire enough for autonomy if that endorsement was produced by manipulation?
Must an autonomous person be able to respond to correct reasons, or is the ability to reason from their own beliefs and desires sufficient?
Can someone remain autonomous while acting against a stable plan or judging that their action is unjustified?
Does causal determination by prior events eliminate self-government, or can agency still operate from the practical point of view?
How should we distinguish an action performed under compulsion from behavior that does not count as action at all?

summaries.example: Maya plans to save her allowance for a bicycle. Her friends suggest spending it on a concert, and she thinks about their reasons before changing her plan. Her choice may still be autonomous, even though it conflicts with her earlier promise. Now imagine that a powerful urge makes resisting nearly impossible, or that someone has trained Maya never to question a certain command. These cases suggest that being influenced is not always the same as losing self-government.
summaries.summary: Personal autonomy is the ability to govern yourself. The entry begins with a puzzle: each agent has authority over their own actions because each agent must initiate whatever they do. Still, people can be moved by influences that seem to defeat this authority. Addiction, brainwashing, coercion, and other forces are examples philosophers use to explore the difference between ordinary influence and autonomy-undermining control. Several theories try to explain the difference. Coherence theories say that a person governs an action when the motive fits with a deeper part of the person’s outlook, such as a higher-order desire, value judgment, plan, care, or character. Reasons-responsive theories require the person to recognize and respond to a suitable range of reasons. Reasoning-based theories emphasize the ability to question one’s motives and draw conclusions from one’s beliefs and desires. Relational theories add that self-respect and self-trust can depend on how a person is treated by others. Incompatibilists argue that autonomy cannot coexist with complete determination by forces beyond the agent’s control; other philosophers think determined actions can still be autonomous if they arise through the agent’s own practical point of view. The entry identifies problems for all these proposals. Someone can be autonomous while acting out of character, abandoning a plan, or making a mistaken choice. The challenge is to explain minimal self-government without requiring perfect wisdom or confusing nonautonomous action with behavior that is not action at all.
key_ideas: Everyone who acts must rely on their own judgment in some way, so agency involves a built-in kind of authority over oneself.
Having authority over your actions is not identical to having effective control over every desire or motive that influences you.
Some philosophers focus on harmony among desires and values; others focus on responding to reasons or reflecting on one’s motives.
Plans and long-term commitments can support self-government, but breaking a plan does not automatically destroy autonomy.
Social experiences can affect autonomy by weakening self-respect or self-trust, even though autonomy is still a person’s own capacity.
The hardest question is finding the minimum needed for self-government without simply describing agency itself or demanding perfect rationality.
summaries.why_it_matters: Autonomy affects how we think about freedom, responsibility, and respect for persons. It helps explain why forcing or manipulating someone is different from persuading them, and why a bad decision is not automatically an unfree one. The topic also connects personal self-rule with political self-rule: both involve rejecting control by an authority that lacks a legitimate right to direct one’s life. Studying the disagreements teaches us that responsibility may depend on the way a motive moves someone, not only on the result.

important_terms.definition: The ability to direct your own actions rather than merely being pushed along by forces that take over your decision-making.
Someone who acts; an agent starts an action and makes decisions about what to do.
A person’s standing power to decide how to act, especially the special authority each agent has over their own actions.
The idea that an action is autonomous when it fits with a person’s deeper wishes, values, plans, or other attitudes.
The ability to notice and be guided by relevant reasons for or against an action.
The ability to examine your own beliefs and desires, decide what follows from them, and revise your motives when your thinking supports revision.
The view that autonomy can be harmed when a person’s ability to form a point of view depends on damaged self-respect or self-trust in social settings.
The position that full causal determination by forces outside an agent’s control is incompatible with autonomy.

questions_to_think_about: When does advice become pressure or control?
Can a person make an autonomous choice that goes against their long-term values?
Should someone lose autonomy because they made a factual mistake?
How might relationships with other people help or harm self-trust?
Does having a cause for every decision prove that the decision was not your own?
